paras: The attempted lynching of George Witherell occurred at Canon City (also printed Canyon City), Colorado, on the night of November 2, 1888, when a crowd that a Pueblo dispatch put at five hundred people met incoming trains at the station intending to lynch Witherell, who was accused of murdering Charles McCain. The crowd searched one train and broke open the baggage car of another, but Witherell was not aboard. The episode appeared as a short item in a few papers, attached to wider coverage of the killing of which Witherell was accused.

According to a Denver dispatch of November 3, Witherell had persuaded McCain, spelled "McKane" in that report, to leave Pueblo with him about a week earlier for the mountains to visit a mining camp. The same dispatch said McCain's mutilated remains were found in Beaver Creek on November 2, and that Witherell had been arrested in Denver when he could not account for McCain's team and a bloody axe was found in his wagon. A Salt Lake Tribune account, reprinted in Butte, dated the killing to October 26 and said Witherell was accused of shooting McCain as he slept in his blankets near Canon City, beating him with an axe and burying the body in a gully. Both reports called Witherell an ex-convict recently released from the Colorado penitentiary after a sentence for killing a sheepherder. The Denver dispatch reported that Witherell was taken to Canon City on the night of November 2 and placed in the penitentiary "as there was talk of lynching him."

A Pueblo dispatch dated November 5 gave the fullest account of the gathering at the Canon City station on Friday night, November 2. Five hundred people were there to meet the trains, on one of which Witherell, printed as "Wetherail," was expected. When the Rio Grande train arrived, it was searched, and the baggagemaster opened his car for inspection. The prisoner was not on the Santa Fe train either, and when its baggagemaster closed his car, the crowd took up railroad ties, smashed the doors and, in the dispatch's words, "almost ruined the car." The dispatch added that the crowd carried a rope and weapons and was fully prepared for a lynching.

Reports differed on where Witherell was that night: the Pueblo dispatch said the sheriff had stopped with the prisoner at Colorado Springs, while the Tribune account said the citizens, "wild with excitement," had taken possession of two trains but that Witherell was being held in Pueblo, where he had been taken before McCain's body was found. A one-line brief in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union placed the gathering on Saturday rather than Friday and said only that the mob was "prepared to lynch the murderer of Charles McCain."
No report of arrests or of any official action against members of the crowd at the station appears in the coverage of this episode.

Coverage came entirely from white papers far from Colorado, and it treated the crowd at the station as a footnote to the killing. The Denver dispatch, which mentioned only "talk of lynching," ran on November 3 and 4 under headlines such as "Killed by a False Friend" in the St. Paul Daily Globe, "Murdered with an Ax" in the Indianapolis Journal and "Shedding Blood for Money" in the New York Sun. The Pueblo account of the station crowd appeared in the Camden Evening Telegram on November 5 under a headline announcing that Witherell had narrowly escaped lynching.

None of these papers questioned the crowd's purpose or Witherell's guilt. The Pueblo dispatch and the Record-Union brief both called him "the murderer" of McCain before any trial, and the Butte Semi-Weekly Miner printed the Tribune's narrative under the headline "Shot While Asleep," telling the killing as established fact and mentioning the attempted lynching only in its closing lines.

The more detailed Pueblo dispatch gives Friday night, November 2, consistent with the Denver report of a move that night; the Record-Union brief gives Saturday. Witherell is placed at Colorado Springs by the Pueblo dispatch, in Pueblo by the Tribune account, and in the Canon City penitentiary by the Denver dispatch, and the coverage does not reconcile these versions.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of George Witherell
bases: A crowd with a rope and weapons searched trains at Canon City to seize and lynch Witherell, accused of murder, but did not find him (A6, A7, A5).

A crowd of about five hundred acting on a murder accusation tried to seize Witherell to lynch him, but he was not found and no one was killed (A6, A7); it is an attempted lynching. His later killing at the Canon City jail on December 4 is a separate episode (see flags).

The Pueblo dispatch (A6), the Salt Lake Tribune account (A7) and the Sacramento brief (A5) independently report a crowd at the Canon City station or trains intent on lynching Witherell, and the Denver wire (A2) reports talk of lynching.
